blocks.text: 1. Hyperparameters

blocks.alt: Set before training starts, hyperparameters control the training process

blocks.text: Iterations, the previous topic, described one precise unit of training progress. Hyperparameters step back to survey the many tunable settings shaping training as a whole, tying together concepts already introduced throughout this entire course.
A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training begins, not learned from data, a genuinely important distinction explored in full depth throughout this topic.
2. Parameters Versus Hyperparameters

blocks.alt: Parameters are learned from data while hyperparameters are set by you

blocks.text: This connects back to weights, already covered throughout Backpropagation & Optimization. Weights are genuinely learned from data during training, adjusted repeatedly through Gradient Descent already covered there.

Hyperparameters are genuinely chosen beforehand, by a human or a search process, entirely different from the weights that Gradient Descent itself adjusts, a genuinely essential distinction covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 3. Examples Already Covered In This Module

This connects back to Learning Rate, Batch Size, and the Number of Epochs, all already covered. Every one of these is genuinely a hyperparameter, chosen before training even starts and held fixed, or adjusted by a schedule, throughout.
These three alone already demonstrate the genuinely wide range of decisions that count as hyperparameters, from how fast weights update to how many examples get grouped together at once.
4. Regularization Hyperparameters

blocks.alt: Regularization hyperparameters include dropout rate and L2 lambda

blocks.text: This connects back to Lambda in L1 and L2 Regularization, the Dropout Rate, and Epsilon in Label Smoothing, all already covered in the Regularization Techniques module. Every one of these regularization strength knobs is also genuinely a hyperparameter.

Each controls how aggressively its own technique regularizes training, and each was already covered as a genuinely tunable value rather than something the network learns on its own through Gradient Descent.
5. Architecture Hyperparameters

blocks.alt: Architecture hyperparameters include number of layers and layer width

blocks.text: This connects back to Network Architecture, already covered in its own topic. Number of layers, number of neurons per layer, and choice of activation function are all genuinely architectural hyperparameters.

These get decided before training begins, and while techniques exist for searching over them too, they are not learned through Gradient Descent the way weights are, exactly the distinction already covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This topic groups together many hyperparameters already covered individually throughout earlier topics in this course. Recognizing them as a single conceptual category is the genuinely useful contribution of this topic.

blocks.text: 6. Why Hyperparameters Genuinely Matter

blocks.alt: Wrong hyperparameters lead to a poor training outcome

blocks.text: A genuinely important, real practical truth follows from everything already covered. The exact same network architecture with genuinely different hyperparameters can produce wildly different training outcomes.

Results can range from genuinely excellent to genuinely broken, entirely due to hyperparameter choices alone, which is exactly why the upcoming Hyperparameter Tuning module treats choosing them well as its own genuinely serious topic.
7. Why Hyperparameters Cannot Be Learned The Same Way

blocks.alt: Hyperparameters get set before gradient descent even starts

blocks.text: This connects back to Gradient Descent, already covered in the Backpropagation & Optimization module. Gradient Descent updates weights using their own gradients, a mechanism already covered in exhaustive detail there.

Hyperparameters have no such gradient with respect to the loss to follow directly, since changing them, like the batch size or the number of layers, alters the entire training process rather than producing a genuinely smooth, differentiable effect on the loss.
8. How Hyperparameters Actually Get Chosen

blocks.alt: Grid or random search finds the best hyperparameters

blocks.text: This connects forward to Grid Search, Random Search, and Bayesian Optimization, all covered in the upcoming Hyperparameter Tuning module. These are systematic search processes that try many combinations of hyperparameters.

They genuinely evaluate which combination actually performs best on validation data, a genuinely different, indirect strategy from the direct gradient-based learning already covered as impossible for hyperparameters in the previous section.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing Why Hyperparameters Deserve This Much Genuine Attention

This connects back to every technique already covered throughout this entire course. Nearly every technique covered so far introduced at least one genuinely important hyperparameter, from activation functions to optimizers to regularization.

This connects forward to the Hyperparameter Tuning module, covered later in this course, where an entire dedicated module exists specifically for choosing these settings well, a direct testament to their genuine practical importance.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates organizing a genuinely typical set of hyperparameters into a single configuration, gathering many concepts already covered throughout this course into one place.

code.content:
hyperparameters = {
    "learning_rate": 0.001,      # already covered throughout Gradient Descent
    "batch_size": 64,             # already covered in Batch Size
    "num_epochs": 20,             # already covered in Epochs
    "l2_lambda": 0.01,            # already covered in L2 Regularization
    "dropout_rate": 0.5,          # already covered in Dropout
    "num_hidden_layers": 3,       # already covered in Network Architecture
    "neurons_per_layer": 128,     # already covered in Network Architecture
    "activation_function": "relu" # already covered in Activation Functions
}

print("A genuinely typical hyperparameter configuration, gathering concepts already covered throughout this course:")
for name, value in hyperparameters.items():
    print(f"  {name}: {value}")

print("\nNone of these values were learned by Gradient Descent. Every one was chosen beforehand, already covered as the core definition in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This configuration is a genuinely realistic starting point, but the exact best values, already covered throughout this topic, genuinely depend on the specific dataset and task, which is exactly why tuning them systematically matters.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training begins, not learned from data.
This is genuinely distinct from parameters, the weights that Gradient Descent learns during training.
Learning Rate, Batch Size, and Number of Epochs are all examples already covered in this module.
Regularization strength knobs, like Lambda, Dropout Rate, and Epsilon, are also hyperparameters.
Architectural choices, like number of layers and activation function, are hyperparameters too.
The same architecture with different hyperparameters can produce wildly different training outcomes.
Hyperparameters have no direct gradient to follow, so they cannot be learned the same way as weights.
Systematic search processes, covered in the upcoming Hyperparameter Tuning module, help choose them well.
Next up: Learning Curves, a genuinely essential tool for visualizing how these choices actually play out during training.
